newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS - Venezuela gasoline price still hot potato. [CORRECTED 23:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Venezuela gasoline price still hot potato. [CORRECTED 23:00 GMT]

text.p: A 27 percent increase in Venezuelan fuel prices Thursday has proved once again to be a lightning rod for protests and discontent in the oil-rich country, analysts said.

Although gasoline prices, at an average 70 bolivars ($0.14) per liter remain five times cheaper (corrects from 20 times cheaper) than a bottle of water, the hike has brought dissent from a wide range of sectors and sparked a bitter dispute between the government and the private sector.
"The gasoline price issue is always a sensitive one and every sector looks to protect itself before public opinion," said Metroeconomica economist Gonzalo Plaz.
To sweeten the impact, the government increased public transport subsidies to prevent bus fares from rising and moved to pressure private sector companies to raise wages.

Hundreds died in a spree of riots and looting in Caracas in February 1989 following a sharp rise in pump prices although a near 500 percent increase in fuel prices last April met with muted public disapproval.

Violent protests have so far not materialized, thanks in large part to the fact that students are on summer vacation. And public transport strikes appear to have been averted by the transport subsidy extension.
Instead the hike has opened a testy debate with business, government and union leaders trading insults and threats.

The Confederation of Venezuelan Workers (CTV), the country's largest union, announced Wednesday a 12-hour national strike for August 6 to protest the higher fuel prices and demand wage rises from the private sector. It would be Venezuela's first national strike for eight years.
Far from condemning the strike call, government ministers have sided with unions and stepped up pressure on businesses by threateneing to raise salaries by decree if they do not comply.
"The government is aware that the labor sector's demands are legitimate," Finance Minister Luis Raul Matos Azocar said Wednesday.

And with December 1998 national elections increasingly in the mind of politicians, public figures from all parties have weighed into the debate criticising both the government for the gasoline price hike and businesses for the tardy wage rises.

The Caracas Stock Exchange, which had been building up an impressive rally, fell 3.2 percent in the first three sessions of the week. Prices picked up 0.6 percent Thursday after the feared violent protests did not materialize.

For markets the gasoline price hike has more of a symbolic than financial importance, bringing fuel prices closer to international levels as written into a stand-by agreement signed with the International Monetary Fund last year.
Business chamber leaders insist that 90 percent of their members have raised salaries and complain that they are being made the scapegoats for the unpopular measure.

"They (government officials) are trying every possible means to confuse public opion and make us responsible," Francisco Natera, head of Venezuela's largest business chamber Fedecamaras, told a news conference Thursday.
The wage dispute originates from an agreement made by a tripartite commission of government, union and business leaders last month to reform labour laws.
Under the accord, which saw the removal of an outdated and burdensome severance payments system, business leaders agreed to raise salaries when their financial situation permitted.
For analysts, the salary debate is counterproductive at a time when cross-sector talks were achieving major breakthroughs and social conflicts were under control.
"It is totally contradictory to carry out a reform to flexibilize the labor market and then threaten an increase in salaries by decree," said independent analyst Orlando Ochoa.

The high initial cost of adapting to a recent 41 percent rise in the minimum salary and the move to new severance payments combined with the still fragile recovery of the economy mean that business must be given time to raise wages, Ochoa said.
"The economic situation of these companies does not allow it. It has to be gradual, the market should decide" he said.
Business, union and government leaders are due to meet Friday to establish whether salaries have been raised and if next Wednesday's strike can be averted.
((-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600))
